To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we have obtained the deepest far- UV images of 15 Lyman-break galaxies (LBGs) at z ~ 2, (2) we have detected 3 of the 15 LBGs at 3σ significance, (3) the escape fraction of Lyman continuum (f_LyC) is less than or equal to 0.05, and (4) the ionizing emissivity of the universe is evolving with time.
the LyC escape fraction is 2.6% ± 1.3% for the starburst galaxy population at z~ 1.3, and the ionizing emissivity at z~1 is a factor of ~3 lower than at z~3.
we have found a statistically significant excess of LyC photons in our deep HST images of starburst galaxies at a redshift of 1.3, and that this excess is consistent with a 10% escape fraction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of optical instruments for astronomy and industry.
the study of the evolution of the universe and the development of its structure.
the study of the physical and chemical processes in the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we do not find evidence of significant LyC escape in these star-forming galaxies at z~1 and, therefore, that the ionizing emissivity of the universe has not changed significantly from z=0.
the LyC escape fraction is < 1.3% for the 15 galaxies observed, which is consistent with the 2.5% upper limit from the Hubble Deep Field.
the escape fraction of ionizing photons is < ~ 1.7% for the 15 galaxies studied, with a 95% confidence level.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the escape fraction of ionizing radiation in starbursts at z ~ 2-3 is likely less than 10%, but may increase to 20% or more at z ~ 6.
we find a very low escape fraction of LyC radiation at z ~ 2.5, but a much higher escape fraction at z ~ 0.3 and 0.6.
there is no evidence for a strong evolution in the ionizing emissivity of galaxies from z ~ 0 to z ~ 1, but the data are consistent with a modest evolution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LyC escape fraction of star-forming galaxies at z ~1.3 is likely to be very low, <~ 1%.
there is evidence for an evolving LyC emissivity, which is consistent with an increasing fraction of galaxies with strong LyC leakage at high redshift.
the LyC escape fraction at z~1-2 is much lower than at lower redshifts.
